name: Newton’s universal gravitation
summary: Newton's Principia (1687) explained falling bodies, the Moon and the planets by one inverse-square attraction between all pieces of matter, uniting earthly and heavenly motion.
description: A single dynamical account relates terrestrial falling bodies, the Moon and planetary motion, with mutually attracting matter and an inverse-square dependence. The proposition extends attraction beyond celestial centres to the material parts of bodies; it is not limited to an inverse-square solar analogy.
tier_reason: Mutual gravitation connects celestial and terrestrial mechanics and underlies later astronomy and engineering calculations across generations.
why: Halley's 1684 question about the orbit produced by an inverse-square force, and Kepler's planetary laws, led Newton to work out a full dynamics.

places.note: England: publication and Whiston; Netherlands: Huygens

market.note: The node is the scientific claim and its scholarly reception, not an individually marketed product.

events.statement: Newton’s Principia linked celestial and terrestrial gravity and extended mutual gravitation to the material parts of bodies.
events.scope: The Principia Book III argument for inverse-square attraction and mutual gravitation extending to the material parts of bodies.
events.caveats: The preserved pages are an excerpt of a large Latin work. Publication does not prove immediate general acceptance or exclusive credit for every component; earlier inverse-square and attraction proposals are separately identified.

events.statement: An unsigned 1688 review, attributed by historians to John Locke, summarized Newton’s mutual attraction of celestial bodies and the extension of gravitation to all material bodies.
events.scope: The 1688 French-language review of the Principia, including the extension of gravitation to all bodies and their equal material particles.
applications: Scholarly review and discussion of celestial and terrestrial dynamics
events.population: John Locke, to whom the unsigned review is attributed by modern scholarship
events.caveats: The periodical review is unsigned at its heading and is attributed to Locke by later scholarship; the author summarizes Newton’s theory without proving he independently verified every demonstration or that all readers accepted it. Earlier recognition is possible.

date.label: By 1690
date.basis: The 1944 editor dates the Discourse’s first publication to January or February 1690; the exact date on which Huygens formed the criticism is not established.

events.statement: Huygens directly discussed Newton’s mutual attraction of material parts and rejected that extension while accepting a celestial centripetal force.
events.scope: Huygens’s critical comparison of Newton’s mutual attraction among material parts with his own account of gravity.
applications: Mathematical and physical criticism of competing gravity theories
events.caveats: The source is an edited 1944 transcription of the 1690 work; the original printed object was not inspected. This is a documented critical engagement, not Huygens’s acceptance of universal attraction, agreement with Newton’s full physics, or proof of first scholarly response.

evidence.supports: States his objection to Newton’s mutual attraction of small parts and accepts the force toward the Sun and Earth in celestial cases.
Dates the first published Discourse to early 1690.

date.basis: ETH dates Whiston’s New Theory to 1696.

events.statement: Whiston placed mutual attraction, universal scope and inverse-square dependence among the premises of his New Theory of the Earth.
events.scope: Whiston’s use of mutually attractive matter and inverse-square dependence as lemmas of his published theory.
applications: Theoretical argument about the Earth and comets
events.caveats: Whiston offered a theological and historical application that is not endorsed here; this single named use does not establish general consensus, independent experimental confirmation, or the first application.

evidence.locator: Book I, printed pp. 2–5 / section PDF pp. 3–6
evidence.supports: States mutual attraction of corpuscles, universal scope and the reciprocal-square dependence.
Connects the work’s third to ninth lemmas and cometary argument to Newton’s Principia.

community_entry.rationale: The review’s specific summary shows a named scholar’s contemporary engagement with the full material-particle proposition; the separate Huygens event preserves an explicit critical response and Whiston’s later event preserves acceptance and use.
community_entry.caveats: The periodical review is unsigned at its heading and is attributed to Locke by later scholarship; the author summarizes Newton’s theory without proving he independently verified every demonstration or that all readers accepted it. Earlier recognition is possible.

caveats: The unsigned 1688 review is attributed to Locke by later scholarship, and it does not prove independent verification of the entire theory. Huygens rejected universal attraction in 1690; Whiston’s later use and prior inverse-square proposals are distinct. Earlier recognition and full global priority are unresolved.
